Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Expectation2: Stay updated on changes in laws and legal precedents.
Situation2: The latest issue of a prominent law review journal has arrived, containing articles on developing legal theories. You want to read them.
Story: I was just settling into my armchair, the latest law review journal in hand, when my phone buzzed. It was Sam, my old college friend. “Hey, can you hop on a quick video call? I’m drowning in these furniture instructions,” he texted, followed by a photo of a half-built bookshelf and a look of utter defeat. I glanced at the journal’s table of contents—an article on a new legal precedent I needed to understand for an upcoming case. As a judge, I’m expected to stay sharp, always up to date, and I’d been looking forward to this quiet hour all week. But Sam rarely asks for help, and I know how much he struggles with these things. My mind raced: if I ignore him, I’m a bad friend. If I put off my reading, I risk falling behind in my professional duties. The weight of both roles pressed on me, each demanding my attention, each unwilling to wait. I stared at my phone, torn, feeling the tension coil tighter inside me.
